text: Metformin traces back to goat's rue (Galega officinalis), a flowering plant used in medieval European folk medicine. Its active compound inspired the drug.
Warfarin's name comes from WARF (Wisconsin Alumni Research Foundation), which funded its discovery, plus “-arin” from coumarin.
Before it became a heart medicine, warfarin was sold as rat poison. Its story began in the 1920s, when cattle bled after eating spoiled sweet clover.
Sildenafil was first studied as a treatment for angina (chest pain). Researchers only noticed its best-known effect during the clinical trials.
“Acetaminophen” (US) and “paracetamol” (Europe) are the same drug. Both names are built from its chemical name, para-acetylaminophenol.
Albuterol (US) and salbutamol (Europe) are exactly the same molecule, just with different official names on each side of the Atlantic.
Atorvastatin (Lipitor) is one of the best-selling drugs in history. For years it was the world's top-selling medicine.
Statins started with fungi: simvastatin is made from a compound produced by the mould Aspergillus terreus.
Omeprazole was the first proton pump inhibitor. It blocks the tiny “pumps” in the stomach lining that release acid.
The same molecule, bupropion, is sold as an antidepressant (Wellbutrin) and as a quit-smoking aid (Zyban).
Allopurinol was developed by Gertrude Elion and George Hitchings, who shared the 1988 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Ibuprofen was discovered in the 1960s by a team at Boots in the UK, led by pharmacologist Stewart Adams.
Amoxicillin belongs to the penicillin family, whose story began in 1928 when Alexander Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria on a forgotten dish.
Azithromycin was discovered in 1980 by chemists at Pliva, a pharmaceutical company in Zagreb, Croatia.
Clopidogrel is a prodrug: it does nothing until the liver converts it. People with certain CYP2C19 gene variants activate it poorly.
Finasteride is sold at one strength for an enlarged prostate (Proscar) and at a much lower strength for hair loss (Propecia).
Prednisone is a prodrug: the liver turns it into prednisolone, the form that actually calms inflammation.
Empagliflozin lowers blood sugar in an unusual way: it makes the kidneys let extra glucose leave the body in urine.
Gabapentin was designed to mimic the brain messenger GABA, but it turns out not to act on GABA receptors at all.
Escitalopram is literally half of citalopram: it is only the “left-handed” mirror-image version (S-enantiomer) of the molecule.
Cetirizine is made in the body from an older antihistamine, hydroxyzine. It is a less drowsy descendant.
Newer antihistamines like loratadine cause less drowsiness because they barely cross from the blood into the brain.
The brand name Lasix is often said to come from “lasts six (hours)”, the typical duration of furosemide's effect.
ACE inhibitors like lisinopril trace back to the venom of a Brazilian pit viper, Bothrops jararaca.
Losartan was the first angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB), approved in the mid-1990s.
Beta-blockers like metoprolol exist thanks to Sir James Black, who received the 1988 Nobel Prize partly for inventing this drug class.
Carvedilol blocks two kinds of receptors, both beta and alpha, which widens blood vessels as well as slowing the heart.
Doxycycline belongs to the tetracyclines, antibiotics first found in Streptomyces, bacteria that live in soil.
Methotrexate is a double-duty drug: high doses treat some cancers, while low weekly doses calm rheumatoid arthritis.
Unlike warfarin, apixaban blocks a single clotting protein (factor Xa) and doesn't need routine INR blood tests.
Fluoxetine (Prozac) reached the US market in 1988 and became one of the most famous medicines of its era.
Sitagliptin was the first DPP-4 inhibitor. It boosts gut hormones that tell the pancreas to release insulin after meals.
Tamsulosin relaxes the smooth muscle around the prostate, which makes it easier to pass urine.
Levothyroxine is a lab-made copy of thyroxine (T4), the hormone your thyroid gland produces naturally.
Zolpidem is one of the “Z-drugs”, a group of sleep medicines whose names happen to start with Z.
Montelukast works by blocking leukotrienes, inflammatory messengers that tighten the airways in asthma.
